title: G-Merging: Graph Models Merging for Parameter-Efficient Multi-Task Knowledge Consolidation
claim: Merging task-specific models is needed, but graph domains are heterogeneous and cross-task transfer is poor; our merge beats naive averaging.
layout: 4 panels left-to-right: task diagram, t-SNE, heatmap, grouped bars
description: A four-panel horizontal strip. Panel 1 is a flow diagram. Task 1 to Task K fine-tuned model boxes in green feed into a yellow 'Merge' oval, then a blue 'Multi-task Model' box. A small molecular graph labeled 'input graph from different tasks' enters that box, and arrows fan out to Task 1 to Task K outputs. Panel 2 is a t-SNE scatter of eight colored clusters, one per molecular dataset, that are visibly separated. Panel 3 is an 8x8 heatmap of ROC scores. Rows are datasets and columns are models. The strong diagonal shows each model does well only on its own task, and the off-diagonal cells are weak. Panel 4 is a grouped bar chart over the eight datasets. Gold bars (Weight Average) are consistently lower than red bars (G-Merging, ours). The eye goes first to the colorful clusters and heatmap, then to the red bars.

(2) A 2D t-SNE visualization of the final-layer embeddings from eight molecular graph datasets, encoded using the graph pre-training model (Hu et al., 2020). abstract: The pretrain-finetuning paradigm has achieved notable success in graph learning. Moreover, merging models fine-tuned on different tasks to enable a parameter-efficient model with multi-task capabilities is gaining increasing attention for its practicality. However, existing model merging methods, such as weight averaging and task arithmetic, struggle to generalize well to graph structures and Graph Neural Network (GNN) models due to the unique structural heterogeneity of graph data. In this paper, we propose an innovative graph model merging framework called G-Merging for merging multiple task-specific fine-tuned GNN models. G-Merging first employs task arithmetic to coarsely merge graph models, capturing shared cross-task knowledge. Second, it introduces a Topology-aware Wasserstein Distance (TWD) loss to train lightweight task adapters, preserving domain-specific graph patterns via aligning the embeddings of merged and fine-tuned models. Third, G-Merging integrates the adapters into a training-free, topology-aware router within a mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture, dynamically routing input graphs to task-specific adapters based on structural similarity, thereby mitigating conflicts and enhancing knowledge sharing. Extensive experiments on 8 graph downstream datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of G-Merging, showing impressive performance close to or exceeding individual finetuned models while improving parameters and training efficiency. Our code is available at https://github.com/cjcj46262/G-Merging.
